title: Kamalakara Pippalai
html:
A Branch of Nityananda

Among the twelve gopalas, the closest companions of Nityananda Prabhu, stands Sri Kamalakara Pippalai — the one to whom the Lord Himself entrusted the service of Sri Jagannatha at Mahesh on the bank of the Ganga. The “Chaitanya-charitamrita” calls him Kamalakara Pippalai and simply Kamalakara; the vandanas call him Pippalai, Pippalai Thakura and Sri Kamalakara; in the “Narottama-vilasa” and the “Prema-vilasa” he is Kamalakara Piplai, and in the “Nityananda-vamsha-vistara,” Pipilai.

Listing the branches of Nityananda’s tree, Krishnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami first speaks of His whole company:

“All of Nityananda’s associates are cowherd friends from Vraja. Each carries a horn and a staff and wears the dress of a cowherd, with a peacock feather on his head.” (CC, Adi 11.21)

And of Kamalakara himself he writes a single line:

“Kamalakara Pippalai was extraordinary in his ways, and his extraordinary love is known throughout the world.” (CC, Adi 11.24)

In the lists of the twelve gopalas he stands third, after Abhirama and Sundarananda and before Gauridasa. Lochana Dasa, in the “Chaitanya-mangala,” naming those who came to earth with the Lord, includes “Sri Kamalakara” among the twelve cowherd boys (gopalas) of Vraja (Sutra-khanda 626–627).

Family and Birthplace

Kamalakara appeared at Khalijuli, a village of the Sundarbans — according to the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” in the Shaka year 1414 (Bengali year 899; 1492 CE).1 He was a brahmana by birth, of the Radhiya brahmanas; “Pippalai” is a family name, counted among the fifty-five “grami” that the Radhiyas bear after the villages of their forefathers. His father, a wealthy landowner, is not named in the biographies. Kamalakara’s younger brother was Nidhipati Pippalai.

Though Khalijuli was his birthplace, he lived at Mahesh, a village on the Ganga in the Hooghly district, some 2½ miles from Srirampur (Serampore). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati says the same in the “Anubhashya,” noting that the temple of Jagannatha at Mahesh is 2½ miles from Srirampur station.2

Jagannatha at Mahesh

How the service of Jagannatha came into Kamalakara’s hands is told in a tradition that Srila Bhaktisiddhanta records in the “Anubhashya.” Once a renunciant Vaishnava (udasina) named Dhruvananda came to Purushottama-kshetra, Puri, with a burning desire to cook bhoga for Sri Jagannatha himself and offer it to the Lord with his own hands. At night Jagannatha came to him in a dream and bade him go to Mahesh, a village on the Ganga, establish His service there and every day offer Him bhoga with his own hands: thus his desire would be fulfilled.3

Dhruvananda came to Mahesh — and saw, approaching him on the waters of the Ganga, Sri Jagannatha with Balarama and Subhadra-devi. The Lord Himself had appeared where He wished to accept service. Dhruvananda reverently lifted the three Deities out of the river, raised a hut for Them on the shore and took up Their service.

As the time of his own departure drew near, one thought filled Dhruvananda’s heart: who would be a worthy servant of Jagannatha? Again the Lord answered him in a dream: the next morning a man of Khalijuli near the Sundarbans, named Kamalakara Pippalai, a great devotee of Jagannatha and the crown of Vaishnavas, would come to Mahesh, and the service was to be entrusted to him. According to tradition, Kamalakara too received the Lord’s command.4 In the morning Dhruvananda met him and handed over to him the service of Sri Jagannatha, Baladeva and Subhadra. From him the Lord’s service at Mahesh descends, and therefore it is said that Kamalakara Pippalai established the Deity of Mahesh; today it is the famous Deity of Jagannatha. Having received the right to serve the Lord, Kamalakara and his family came to be called Adhikari, and the family bears that name to this day.

The biographies see in this story a law of bhakti: only a devotee’s service does the Lord accept, and a devotee counts the chance to serve Vishnu and the Vaishnavas his highest wealth. The Lord Himself shows how to serve Him to one who longs for it with all his heart; but one attached to sense enjoyment sees service as a burden and looks for ways to avoid it.

And Kamalakara had come to Mahesh in this way: as soon as he received Sri Jagannatha’s command, he at once left his home and all his relatives. In this there was neither flight from duty nor harsh austerity. A devotee, even when he plays the role of a householder, is not like a worldly family man: his mind is ever immersed in viraha, the pain of being apart from the Lord, and at a single word from Him he gladly leaves worldly ties for the sake of service. Such renunciation comes of itself, naturally, not forced as with jnanis and yogis; and at times the Lord Himself wishes His devotee to remain in family life.

Nor was Kamalakara’s family abandoned. A second tradition preserved in the “Anubhashya” tells that his younger brother Nidhipati searched for him long and found him at Mahesh. Unable to persuade Kamalakara to return home, he at last settled at Mahesh himself, bringing both his own family and Kamalakara’s.

According to the “Vaishnavachara-darpana,” Kamalakara lived at Mahesh on the western bank of the Ganga, served the Deity of Jagannatha there and glorified Radha and Krishna in song day and night. One of the biographies adds that before he came the country around Mahesh was jungle: he cleared the land and founded an exemplary settlement, famed far and wide.

Descendants and Jagannatha’s Land

Kamalakara’s line, according to the “Anubhashya,” is this: his son was Chaturbhuja, who had two sons, Narayana and Jagannatha; Jagadananda was born to Narayana, and Rajiva-lochana to Jagadananda.5 To this day some thirty brahmana families of his line live at Mahesh, among them Sri Prasadadasa Adhikari.6 His descendants, as the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” writes, serve Jagannatha at Mahesh.

In Rajiva-lochana’s time the means for Jagannatha’s service ran short. Then, in the Bengali year 1060 (1653 CE), the Nawab of Dhaka — apparently Shah Shuja — made a gift of 1185 bighas to Jagannathadeva, in a village a krosha and a half west of Mahesh; the mauza was named after the Lord — Jagannathpur.7

A mile north of Mahesh lies Vallabhapura, the shripata of Rudra Pandita (Rudrarama), whose Deity is Radha-vallabha. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes that formerly, at Ratha-yatra, Jagannatha of Mahesh used to visit the temple of Radha-vallabha at Vallabhapura; but from the Bengali year 1262 (1855–1856), owing to quarrels among the servitors, the custom ceased.

Daughter and Granddaughter

The sources speak differently of Kamalakara’s daughter. The “Nityananda-vamsha-vistara” begins its account of Virachandra’s line thus:

“In Mahesh there lived a brahmana of pure heart; the worship of Vishnu and the Vaishnavas was his daily duty. His name was Sudhamaya; he was the son-in-law of Pipilai, and his wife was named Vidyunmala.” (“Nityananda-vamsha-vistara” 3.3–4)

By this account Vidyunmala was Kamalakara’s daughter and Sudhamaya of Mahesh his son-in-law.8 The couple had no children, and Narayani became their daughter: according to the “Nityananda-vamsha-vistara,” she was given to them by the Ocean. Narayani became the wife of Sri Virabhadra Prabhu, Nityananda’s son. The Adhikaris of Mahesh, descendants of the Pippalai line, call this girl Radharani.9

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati writes otherwise: Virabhadra married Shrimati, born to Yadunatha Acharya of the village of Jhamatpur in the Hooghly district and his wife Vidyunmala (Lakshmi), and also their adopted daughter Narayani. That Vidyunmala was Kamalakara’s daughter Srila Bhaktisiddhanta does not say outright. The “Vaishnavachara-darpana,” for its part, relates that Vidyunmala was given in marriage to a worthy brahmana, Yadunandana, whose father-in-law was a great devotee of Jagannatha who knew no desire but to serve Jagannatha.

With Nityananda and Jahnava

Kamalakara’s shripata at Akna-Mahesh, near Srirampur, became the scene of one of the wonders of sankirtana. Once, while harinama-sankirtana was going on there, godless men flung a jackal’s carcass into the circle of singers — and by the power of Parameshvari Dasa’s kirtana the jackal revived.

According to one tradition, Kamalakara was great in the irrepressibility of his bhava, and Nityananda gave him the village of Panihati.10 Jayananda, telling of the wonders of Nityananda’s companions after the Lord’s disappearance, calls Kamalakara’s “madness of prema” great: overwhelmed by ecstasy, he did not notice even the wounds on his own body and did not return to outward consciousness.11 This was no worldly derangement, but the self-forgetfulness of a cowherd boy of Vraja in love for the Lord.

He was also at the famous chida-dadhi festival at Panihati arranged by Raghunatha Dasa, which the biographies call the Danda-mahotsava.12 Krishnadasa Kaviraja, naming the close companions who sat around Nityananda on the raised platform, names him as well:

“Ramadasa, Sundarananda, Gadadhara Dasa, Murari, Kamalakara, Sadashiva, Purandara…” (CC, Antya 6.61)

In the “Anubhashya” on this verse Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that this is the same Kamalakara spoken of in Adi 11.24.

Kamalakara attended the festival at Katwa given by Gadadhara Dasa as well. And when Narottama Thakura called the Vaishnavas to the great Kheturi festival, Kamalakara went there from Kharadaha in the retinue of Jahnava-devi. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” names him among her companions: “Sri Shankara, Sri Kamalakara Pippalai, Nrisimha, Chaitanya, Jiva, Pandita Kanai” (BR 10.375). His name also appears in the “Narottama-vilasa” — among those whom the news of the gathering of Vaishnavas reached (6.188), among the mahantas who sat down to the feast in Jahnava’s courtyard on the festival’s second day (8.51) and among those whom Ishvari, Jahnava-devi, told to return to Kharadaha (8.152–153); the “Prema-vilasa” mentions him too (19.309).

Narahari Chakravarti, in the “Namamrita-samudra,” where his prayers call upon the Lord's associates, addresses him together with Mahesha Pandita:

“Sri Kamalakara Piplai, O Mahesha, hear me! Deliver this unworthy one, and your fame will be proclaimed without end.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 37)

Departure

According to the “Vaishnavachara-darpana,” once his daughter was married, Kamalakara went to Vrindavana-dhama and, living there, disappeared from view. The Adhikaris of Mahesh keep a tradition that he left this world in the Shaka year 1485 (Bengali year 970; 1563 CE), at the age of seventy-one, on the shukla-trayodashi of the month of Chaitra (by the Vaishnava reckoning, the month of Vishnu).13 No primary source for these dates is named, and our calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math has no days of Kamalakara Pippalai’s appearance or disappearance.

Mahabala

Who Kamalakara was in Krishna’s eternal pastimes Kavi Karnapura reveals in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika”:

“Subala, the best of the dear friends, is Gauridasa Pandita; the mighty Mahabala is Kamalakara Pippalai.” (GGD 128)

So he is called by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” — “one of the twelve gopalas, Mahabala” — and by the “Vaishnavachara-darpana”: the cowherd boy Mahabala of Vrindavana has now come as Kamalakara Pippalai. A cowherd friend of Vraja, in Gaura’s pastimes too he remained a companion of Nityananda — of Balarama.

The vandanas remember in him just this cowherd, childlike mood. Devakinandana praises “Kamalakara Pippalai, sporting in bhava, who said to the Lord: ‘Take the stick, give me the flute’” (Devakinandana’s “Vaishnava-vandana,” 96) — the words of a cowherd friend of Vraja. The Sanskrit vandana attributed to Srila Jiva Gosvami honours “Pippalai, overwhelmed by a childlike mood” (100); the tripadi vandana, “Thakura Pippalai, artless in a child’s feeling, all of whose pastimes and play are like a child’s” (85); and beside him in both stands Kamalakara Dasa — he “whose bliss is sankirtana” (100), and “whose highest exultation is in the sankirtana of Krishna” (86).14 In Devakinandana’s Sanskrit list of the names of Vaishnavas “Sri Kamalakara” is named among the associates as well (32).

The extraordinary conduct and extraordinary love of which Krishnadasa Kaviraja speaks are the love of Mahabala, the friend of Krishna and Balarama. Its fruit has remained in the world: at the Lord’s command Kamalakara left everything to serve Him, and Jagannatha of Mahesh, who chose His servant Himself, accepts service from his line to this day.

Notes

  1. Another biography, citing the “Shripata-paryatana,” says that he was born at Akna-Mahesh and lived at Jageshvara, naming Khalijuli in the Sundarbans as his birthplace only “according to other sources.” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta calls Kamalakara “a resident of Khalijuli.”
  2. According to another biography, about two miles from Serampore station.
  3. The biographies do not identify this Dhruvananda with Dhruvananda Brahmachari of the branch of Gadadhara Pandita (CC, Adi 12.79); the two should not be confused.
  4. In the “Anubhashya” only Dhruvananda has the prophetic dream. One of the biographies adds that Jagannatha told him: “In a dream I have bidden him come here and accept My service,” and that Kamalakara did have such a dream.
  5. One of the biographies omits Jagadananda and names Rajiva-lochana as Narayana’s son. This Jagadananda should not be confused with Jagadananda Pandita, the associate of Mahaprabhu.
  6. According to another biography, the descendants of the line around Mahesh number some twenty families.
  7. In the “Anubhashya” the Nawab’s name is given with a query: “Oyalish Sa (Suja?)”. Another biography gives “Wali Shah Shuja” and places Jagannathpur about two and a half kroshas from the temple at Mahesh.
  8. In the “Nityananda-vamsha-vistara” (3.7) Sudhamaya is called Mukhuti (Mukhopadhyaya); the biographies call him Sudhamaya Chattopadhyaya.
  9. So according to one of the biographies; another, citing the same Adhikaris, says only that “the daughter” was called Radharani, without specifying whether Vidyunmala or Narayani is meant.
  10. The biographies cite these words from a “Vijaya-khanda” without naming its author; in the fragments of Jayananda’s “Vijaya-khanda” known to us there is no such couplet. The line itself is built like the verse of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” about Kamalakanta Pandita, to whom Nityananda gave Saptagrama (CB, Antya 5.729), and Panihati, according to the “Charitamrita” and the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” is the home of Raghava Pandita. The source of this tradition has not been established.
  11. Jayananda’s words are: “Great was the madness of prema of Kamalakara Pippalai: he cut his own body, and yet he did not come to himself.” So the poet expresses the depth of ecstatic self-forgetfulness; this is neither self-mortification nor an example to imitate.
  12. According to one of the biographies, this festival took place in the Shaka year 1439 (1517 CE); the “Charitamrita” gives no year.
  13. According to another biography, the date of his departure is the same shukla-trayodashi of Chaitra, 1563. How this year accords with his presence at the Kheturi festival the sources do not explain.
  14. Whether Pippalai and Kamalakara Dasa of the neighbouring verses of the vandanas are one person is unclear. Another vandana calls “Kamalakara Pandita,” to whom Nityananda gave Saptagrama, Vasudama; this confuses him with Kamalakanta Pandita of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Antya 5.729), and it disagrees with the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” (Vasudama is Dhananjaya, GGD 127; Mahabala is Kamalakara Pippalai, GGD 128).
